pr.title: Give each project page a summary's sidebar
pr.head: d177d5c5fbd0787f0593a556f6437d07739ab1c1

summary: Projector's site has two kinds of page that describe the same work. A project page renders one plan from docs/projects/. A summary page walks through one pull request, with a sidebar that lists the pull request's whole stack under segment headers: each header names the project that a run of the stack's layers carries out, and links to that project's page.

Before this change, a project page showed its plan under a small head with a flat line of review links, and a tree of its folder in a column at the window's edge. So the project's view left out stack order, layers with no summary, and layers of the same stack that carry out another project. A reader who moved from a project to one of its pull requests met two different pictures of one piece of work.
This change gives every project page the summary page's layout and the summary page's sidebar, drawn by the same code:

1. The build lists each project's stacks. site.json gives each project stacks: the segments of every stack that holds a segment it heads, newest first. It replaces the old reviews list.
  2. One renderer draws both sidebars. sideNavHtml in summary.ts draws the box, its stacks, a middle part, and a footer row. The summary page passes its sections and versions, and the project page passes its other pages and a history link.
  3. A project page takes the summary layout. A title row holds the breadcrumbs, badges, owner, and View on GitHub above the plan's title, and the plan's own first <h1> leaves the body. An HTML page keeps its full-window frame, with the sidebar in its collapsible column.
The pull request also marks the project-page-nav plan completed and records its outcome.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Stack: pull requests that sit on one another, each based on the branch of the one below.
  • Segment: a run of a stack's layers that carry out one project, bottom first. A stack where no layer names a project is one segment headed by a title.
  • Header: a segment's heading in the sidebar, a StackHeader. A project's header links to its page; a title is plain text.
  • Current: the item that is the page you are on. A sidebar marks exactly one with aria-current="page".
  • Title row: the summary page's <header class="top">, an eyebrow line above an <h1>.

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html:
• A Projector review of this head found no blocking issue.
  • The compiled JavaScript matches the TypeScript, and the 754 Python tests pass.
  • One suggestion: a sentence about the Docs sidebar in docs/cli.md still says "Each sidebar", which now reads as if it covered project pages.

groups.title: site.json lists each project's stacks
groups.kicker: The data contract the project sidebar reads, and the build step that fills it
intro: The site's front end draws every page from site.json, which build_site writes. Each project in it carried reviews, the numbers of the summarized pull requests whose segment the project heads. That list lost the stack's order and every layer without a summary.

Each project now carries stacks, a list of stacks, newest first, where each stack is the same segments list every summary page of that stack already carries: a header and its members, bottom first, with unsummarized layers included. Because both views read one value, a project's sidebar and its pull requests' sidebars cannot disagree, and the build asks GitHub for nothing new.

checks.text: A stack appears once under each project any of its headers names. So a stack whose layers carry out projects A and B shows, whole, on both project pages.

files.note: Each Reviews index entry gains segments, and the new project_stacks files each stack under the projects its headers name.

checks.text: Each stack is taken exactly once. stack_groups puts the lowest summarized member first in each group, and build_summaries sets that entry's stack to its own number, or to None when it is the only summarized member. I traced both paths, including a stack whose bottom layer has no summary.
Proposed projects are in described here, and their headers come from the same headers map, so a proposed project's page gets its stacks too.

files.note: The types: StackRow for one pull request's row, SideNav for everything a sidebar is drawn from, and stacks in place of reviews.

checks.text: No reader of a project's reviews field remains in src/ or site/src/; I searched both. The top-level reviews list in site.json, the Reviews index, is unchanged.

groups.title: One renderer draws both sidebars
groups.kicker: The shared helpers at the top of summary.ts, and the styles they need
intro: Every page of the site loads summary.js before site.js, so the functions at the top level of summary.ts are shared helpers both pages call. This group moves the whole sidebar there.

• sideNavHtml(nav) draws the box: one stackgroup per stack, or nav.empty when there is none, then nav.middle, then the footer row with the credit and nav.foot.
  • stackSegmentsHtml gains current, a project name, and mark. A header that names current is highlighted and drawn as plain text, and only the first one carries aria-current when mark is true.
  • titleRowHtml draws the title row that renderPage used to write inline.
The summary page's own output stays the same apart from the new stackgroup wrapper around its one stack, because it passes current: ''.

files.note: The shared helpers, and renderPage rewritten to call them.

checks.text: A project readme's sidebar holds exactly one aria-current. sideNavHtml passes mark only to the first stack with a current header, and stackSegmentsHtml marks only that stack's first such header. ProjectPageTests.drawn asserts the count on every page it draws.
ICON moves to the top level so site.ts can drop its copy. Both files are classic scripts, so a top-level const in summary.js is visible to site.js.

files.note: Styles for a current header, the divider between stacks, the empty line, and the history link, each scoped under .prblock or .navfoot.

groups.title: A project page takes a summary's layout
groups.kicker: How site.ts frames a project page and builds its sidebar
intro: frame draws every view of the site. It gains top and nav. With top, it draws the summary layout: a site bar that scrolls away, a 1440-pixel wrap, the title row, and a grid of the 250-pixel sidebar beside the content column. Without it, it draws the old layout, with nav as an HTML page's collapsible column.

showProjectFile builds the title row and calls the new projectNav, which turns the project's stacks into rows. A layer with a summary links to its review; one without links to the pull request on GitHub with an empty title. Below the stacks it lists the project's own pages with tree, the function that draws the docs tree.

Because the sidebar now sits inside the main element, the docs tree's old rules, written as .sitemain .side, would have restyled it. They now name the column as the main element's child, and the tree's list and link rules name a new sidetree class.

checks.text: On a readme, the project's own headers are current and plain text. On a supplemental or HTML page, current is empty, the headers link back to the readme, and the file's entry in the pages list is current instead.

files.note: frame's new layout, the first-heading removal, and projectNav.

checks.text: The plan's first element leaves only when it is an <h1>. A plan that opens with a paragraph keeps its heading, so its title shows twice.
An HTML page keeps its old head of breadcrumbs and View on GitHub above its frame, because the frame fills the window and has no room for a title row.
Every value the sidebar and title row insert, including titles, URLs, and the owner, passes through esc. test_a_project_title_is_escaped covers a title.

files.note: The withnav layout, the badges in the eyebrow, the column rules rescoped to .sitemain > .side, and .sidetree.

checks.text: The docs tree looks as it did. .sidetree ul restores the 12-pixel indent for nested lists, and the top-level list stays flush. .sidetop a is muted, which is what the old, more specific .sitemain .side a made it.

groups.title: Compiled JavaScript

checks.text: In site/, npm ci, npm run check, and npm run build left both files unchanged at this head.

groups.title: Tests
groups.kicker: Build tests for stacks, and page tests that run the compiled code under node
intro: SiteContentTests checks each project's stacks in site.json. The new ProjectPageTests runs the compiled showProjectFile under node, against a stub DOM, and checks the layout, the title row, the first-heading removal, and the sidebar. TreeColumnStyleTests reads site.css to check the rescoped rules.

checks.text: All 754 tests pass at this head under Python 3.12.

groups.title: Documentation and the plan
groups.kicker: The CLI reference's site section, and the plan's outcome
intro: docs/cli.md describes the project page as it now draws. The project-page-nav plan moves to completed, and its new § 8, Outcome, records that it shipped, the browser checks the author ran, and four details the implementation settled.

files.note: The project page paragraph, and the proposed project paragraph's banner and history link.

checks.text: Around line 789, the Docs paragraph still says "Each sidebar lists its readme as Overview and appears only when there is more than that readme to list". A project's sidebar now always shows and leaves its readme to the headers, so a reader can misapply that sentence. Saying "The Docs sidebar" would fix it.
completed makes no readiness claim, so the plan's open questions do not gate the review.
